title: How to Get Over a Broken Heart: 9 Steps That Really Help
h1: How to Get Over a Broken Heart: 9 Steps That Really Help You Heal
description: How to get over a broken heart, one honest step at a time: feel the pain, change old habits, move your body, lean on support and rebuild a life you love.
keyword: how to get over a broken heart
excerpt: Heartbreak hurts in your whole body. These 9 practical, compassionate steps help you get through the worst days and slowly build a life that feels like yours again.
intro:
Heartbreak isn’t only an emotional experience. It can steal your appetite, wreck your sleep, and make a song in the grocery store feel like a punch. If you’re wondering how to get over a broken heart, the first thing to know is that what you’re feeling is normal, and it won’t feel this way forever.

There’s no shortcut through grief, but there are things that make the road shorter and gentler. Below are 9 steps that help, whether your heart was broken by a breakup, a divorce, unrequited love or a relationship that simply faded. Take what’s useful, leave the rest, and go at your own pace.
body:
1. Let yourself feel the pain

It’s tempting to numb heartbreak: stay busy every waking second, scroll until 3 a.m., jump straight into a rebound, or insist you’re “totally fine.” Avoidance might work for a few days, but feelings you push down tend to resurface later, often at worse moments.

Instead, give your grief some room. Cry if you need to. Write a messy journal entry. Tell a friend, “I’m really not okay today.” Acknowledging the loss is not wallowing. It’s how your mind starts to process what happened.

A helpful approach is to schedule your sadness. Give yourself 20 or 30 minutes a day to feel it fully, then do something grounding afterward, like a shower, a walk or a meal. This keeps grief from swallowing your whole day while still honoring it.

2. Accept that it’s over (even if you don’t understand why)

Part of what keeps hearts broken is the endless search for an explanation. Why did they leave? What did I do wrong? What if I’d said something different? You may never get answers that satisfy you, and that’s painful.

Acceptance doesn’t mean you agree with what happened or that it didn’t hurt. It means you stop fighting reality. Try saying it plainly to yourself: “This relationship ended. I’m sad, and I’m going to be okay.” You may need to repeat it many times before it sinks in. That’s normal.

You don’t need closure from them to move on

Many people hold out for one final conversation that will make everything make sense. Sometimes that conversation helps. Often it doesn’t, because your ex may not fully understand their own reasons, or may not be able to say them in a way that eases your pain. Closure is something you can give yourself. Try writing a letter to your ex that you never send. Say everything: what you loved, what hurt, what you wish had been different, and what you’re ready to release. Read it aloud, then put it away or tear it up. It sounds simple, but putting the story into your own words is a powerful way to close the chapter on your terms.

3. Create some distance

It’s very hard to heal from someone while you’re still watching their stories, rereading old texts or texting “just to check in.” Every bit of contact can reopen the wound.

  • Mute or unfollow them on social media, at least for now. You can decide about friendship later.
  • Archive old messages and photos so they aren’t a tap away.
  • Put reminders in a box. You don’t have to throw them out, just out of sight.
  • Limit contact to necessary logistics if you share a home, pets, kids or a workplace.

If you find your thoughts looping back to them constantly, our guide on how to stop thinking about your ex has more strategies.

4. Change the habits that keep you stuck

Relationships weave themselves into routines. The coffee shop you went to together, the show you watched on Sunday nights, the side of the bed you slept on. These cues trigger memories over and over.

Gently reshape your routines. Try a new café, rearrange your furniture, swap your Sunday show for a call with a friend or a new hobby. Small changes signal to your brain that a new chapter has started. They also make space for experiences that belong only to you.

5. Move your body

Exercise won’t fix heartbreak, but it’s one of the most reliable ways to ease the stress, restlessness and low mood that come with it. Physical activity can improve sleep, burn off anxious energy and give you a sense of accomplishment on days when everything else feels hard.

You don’t need an intense program. A brisk walk, a dance class, yoga, a bike ride or lifting weights all count. Choose something you can do consistently, and notice how you feel afterward. Exercising outside, especially in green spaces, can feel extra restorative.

6. Feed your mind with something hopeful

When your inner voice is harsh, it helps to borrow better words for a while. Reading books about resilience, self-compassion or personal growth can give you perspective and comfort. So can memoirs from people who rebuilt their lives after loss, podcasts on healing, or even uplifting fiction that reminds you life is bigger than this moment.

Try to limit the content that keeps you stuck, such as sad playlists on repeat or videos analyzing your ex’s zodiac sign at midnight. A little catharsis is fine. A steady diet of it isn’t.

7. Build a strong support system

Heartbreak can make you want to hide, but isolation tends to make it worse. Let a few trusted people in. Tell them what you need, whether that’s a distraction, a listening ear or someone to make sure you’re eating.

  • Plan regular check-ins with friends or family, even short ones.
  • Say yes to some invitations, even if you leave early.
  • Look for new connections through classes, clubs or volunteering.
  • Consider a support group if you’re going through a divorce or major loss.

If you’re feeling especially isolated, read our guide on how to deal with loneliness.

Tip: If weeks pass and you still can’t sleep, eat or function, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself, talk to a licensed therapist or your doctor. In the US, you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline any time.

If you’re shy about reaching out

Asking for support can feel awkward, especially if you’re naturally reserved or you’re used to being the strong one. Start small. A simple text works: “Hey, I’ve been having a rough time since the breakup. Would you be up for a walk this week?” Most people are glad to help when they know you need it. You can also find comfort in lower-pressure settings, like online communities, journaling or a therapist, where you can open up at your own pace.

8. Be kind to yourself about the timeline

There’s no correct amount of time to heal. Some people feel better in weeks, others take many months, and progress is rarely a straight line. You might have a great week and then fall apart over a random memory. That doesn’t mean you’re back at square one.

Speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend going through the same thing. Self-compassion isn’t self-pity. It’s choosing patience over judgment. Basic self-care helps too: regular meals, water, sleep, fresh air, and saying no to things that drain you.

9. Rediscover who you are on your own

A breakup leaves a gap, but it also leaves room. What did you set aside during the relationship? Which interests, friends or dreams faded into the background? This is a chance to reconnect with them.

Set a few small goals that excite you: learn a skill, plan a solo trip, train for a 5K, redecorate your space, sign up for a class. Each one builds confidence and reminds you that your life is yours. Over time, you’ll notice your thoughts drifting toward your future more than your past.

For more ideas, browse things to do to move on from a breakup and our guide on how to be happy with yourself.

The bottom line on healing a broken heart

Getting over a broken heart isn’t about forgetting someone or pretending they didn’t matter. It’s about slowly building a life that feels full without them. Feel the pain, create some distance, care for your body, lean on people who love you and be patient with yourself. One day you’ll realize you went a whole afternoon without thinking about them, and then a whole week. That’s healing, and it’s coming.

When you’re ready for more support, explore our full collection of breakup advice.
takeaways: Let yourself grieve instead of numbing the pain; acknowledging it is how healing starts.
Create distance from your ex online and offline so the wound can close.
Exercise, new routines and a strong support system ease the hardest days.
Healing isn't linear, so be patient and kind with yourself about the timeline.

faq.q: How long does it take to get over a broken heart?
faq.a: There’s no set timeline. It depends on the length and depth of the relationship, how it ended, and the support you have. Some people feel noticeably better within a few weeks, while others take many months. Steady progress, rather than a specific date, is the best sign you’re healing.

faq.q: Why does a broken heart physically hurt?
faq.a: Emotional pain and stress affect the body. Heartbreak can disrupt sleep and appetite, trigger stress hormones and leave you feeling tense, tired or achy. These symptoms usually ease with time and self-care. If physical symptoms are severe or don’t improve, check in with a doctor.

faq.q: Should I stay friends with my ex after a breakup?
faq.a: Friendship can work later, but it’s usually easier to heal first. Take some time with little or no contact so feelings can settle. If you eventually try friendship, make sure it’s because you genuinely value it, not because you’re hoping to get back together.

faq.q: Is it okay to date again while I’m heartbroken?
faq.a: It’s okay whenever you genuinely feel ready, but using a new person to numb the pain can hurt you both. A good test is whether you’re excited to know someone new, or mainly trying to fill a gap. If it’s the second, give yourself a little more time.
